newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota low-emission cars to use more platinum.
newsitem.headline: Toyota low-emission cars to use more platinum.

text.p: Toyota Motor Corp plans to introduce low-emission vehicle models later this year that will use more platinum group metals in their autocatalysts than existing models, a senior Toyota executive said.

"From the end of this year we will start introducing cars equipped with a new exhaust system that can reduce emissions of carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxide to only one-10th of levels (currently allowed under Japanese regulations)," Akihiro Wada, an executive vice president in charge of product research and development, told Reuters in a recent interview.
He did not specify how much additional platinum group metal would be used in the new autocatalysts.
Toyota's low-emission engine will be available on most of its mainstay models beginning with the 1998 model year, Wada said.

The system is similar to one developed by Honda Motor Co Ltd in which the catalytic converter is located close to the exhaust manifold to boost its effectiveness immediately after the engine is started.

In February, Honda introduced low emission vehicle (LEV) versions of its Civic Ferio four-door sedan and Partner commercial van in Japan with emission levels only one-10th of current regulatory limits for carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxide.
Honda said those models were equipped with a 400-cell catalytic converter containing platinum and palladium, compared with conventional 300-cell converters.

Although Toyota did not disclose the additional volume of platinum group metals to be used in its LEV models, industry sources expected the Toyota cars' converters would be bigger than Honda's, as Honda engines tend to offer greater combustion control than Toyota engines do.

Asked if Toyota planned to increase the use of aluminium and magnesium in its cars, Wada said: "We will increase the use of aluminium (to improve fuel efficiency), but increases in the use of magnesium will be slow because of poor corrosion resistance."
